chunks: Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, from Ayyub ibn Nuh, from Safwan, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, who said: Al-Husayn ibn Musa al-Hannat narrated to me; he said:
I asked Aba 'Abd Allah عليه السلام about a man who drinks wine, then spits it out from his mouth and it strikes my garment. He said: There is no harm.

Thus, the sound approach regarding all these reports is that we carry them upon a mode of taqiyyah, because they accord with the doctrines of many of the 'ammah. We only said that because the earlier reports conform to the outward sense of the Qur'an.
Allah, Exalted is He, said: “Indeed, wine, gambling, idols, and divining arrows are filth.”
So He judged wine to be impurity.

key_terms.التَّقِيَّةِ: dissimulation or precautionary concealment in circumstances requiring it
key_terms.الْخَمْرَ: wine; the intoxicant under discussion in the ruling
key_terms.الْعَامَّةِ: the broader Sunni public or non-Imami majority in this context
key_terms.الْقُرْآنِ: the Qur'an, cited here as the basis for preferring one set of reports
key_terms.بِالرَّجَاسَةِ: as impurity; the legal implication drawn from the verse
key_terms.ثَوْبِي: my garment; the clothing affected by contact with the wine
key_terms.رِجْسٌ: filth or impurity, used in the verse to characterize wine
key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ: there is no harm; a phrase indicating apparent permissibility or no problem

ai.seo_question: How do Shia hadith interpret reports about wine touching clothing, and why are some understood as taqiyyah?
ai.summary: This report discusses the ruling on wine contacting clothing and then explains that certain reports indicating leniency are to be understood as issued under taqiyyah. The passage supports the impurity of wine by appealing to the apparent meaning of the Qur'anic verse describing wine as rijs.
